records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) field carries four alphabetized entries (Harlequin Blueflag, Large Blue Iris, Larger Blue Flag Iris, Northern Blue Flag) in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so the name it leads with is 'Harlequin Blueflag'; its own body prose instead opens by calling the species 'Larger blue flag iris.' MoBot's displayed Common Name field carries a single value, 'blue flag'; a longer Common Names list exists only inside the popup link's markup, so it is not quoted here, and MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose separately calls the species 'northern blue flag.' RHS's H1 is the bare binomial 'Iris versicolor', with the plant-profile subtitle and page title giving 'blue flag', and its Other common names list adds Boston iris, liver lily, North American blue flag, particoloured iris, purple iris, snake lily and wild iris. Because RHS and MoBot are both dedicated single-species pages and both lead with 'blue flag', that name is used here as common_name, with 'Larger Blue Flag Iris' (NC State's prose) and 'Northern Blue Flag' (MoBot's prose, and NC State's fourth listed entry) noted as the competing forms. NC State's 'Iris versicolor is often confused with:' module lists Iris pseudacorus, Iris tridentata and Iris virginica, distinguishing this species from I. virginica and from the invasive lookalike I. pseudacorus; I. germanica is not listed in that module. Distinct from Iris germanica (Bearded Iris) and Iris cristata (Dwarf Crested Iris) already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (Poisonous to Humans heading, i.e. human-scoped) rates this species Poison Severity: Low, with Poison Symptoms: "CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Nausea, salivation, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, diarrhea, elevated temperature following ingestion; skin irritation upon contact with seeds, rootstock, or cell sap. Highest concentration in rhizomes." Poison Toxic Principle is given as "Pentacylic terpenoids (zeorin, missourin and missouriensin), Irisin, iridin, or irisine," Causes Contact Dermatitis is "Yes," and the full Poison Part list is "Roots / Sap/Juice / Seeds" (never truncated to Leaves). NC State's Plant Type list separately carries the co-listed trait "Poisonous" alongside Bulb, Perennial, and Wildflower. Distinct from that human-scoped Poison block, NC State's Problems tags separately mark the species "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" — the basis for toxic_to_pets=true, since both cats and dogs are named. RHS's Botanical Details carries a "Potentially harmful" field reading in full "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants"; its Pets line is scoped to pets generically (not cats/dogs specifically) and is disclosed here as corroboration only, not as the basis for the cat/dog determination. Missouri Botanical Garden adds its own hazard statement in Noteworthy Characteristics, "Rhizome is poisonous.", and its own handling instruction in Culture, "Wear gloves when dividing the rhizomes."
unknowns: No admissible source gives a numeric soil pH range for Iris versicolor: NC State's page carries no Soil pH field at all, and RHS's Growing Conditions field states only the qualitative 'Acid or Neutral,' with no numeric band to check in either direction, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null.

No admissible source frames watering for this species as a dry-down/interval or depth-check regime (it is an in-ground marsh/pond perennial), so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null per the rule for in-ground perennials.

No admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule, strength, or active-month window specific to Iris versicolor, so fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null.

No admissible source gives indoor day/night temperature targets, humidity percentages, or foot-candle light levels for this species (all three sources describe it as a hardy outdoor aquatic/bog perennial, zones 3-9 per NC State, RHS Hardiness not fetched as a numeric H-rating in the visible text), so day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, and direct_sun_hours_max are all left null; NC State's Light field text '(6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is that field's generic site-wide legend wording, not species-specific prose, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max.

chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note are left null: no admissible source states a numeric cold-damage onset temperature (only USDA hardiness zone ranges, which are survival ratings, not damage-onset figures) or a cool-rest/dormancy watering instruction.

RHS's 'Potentially harmful... Pets: Harmful if eaten' note is scoped to pets generically, naming no specific animal, so it was not used to support toxic_to_pets=true; NC State's cats/dogs/horses-scoped Problems tags were used instead, per the cat/dog scoping rule.

is_houseplant is inferred as false from the consistent outdoor/aquatic-bog cultivation picture across all three sources (RHS: Aquatic, Bogs, Herbaceous Perennial; NC State: pond/water-garden landscape use, USDA zones 3a-9b; MoBot: marginal aquatic perennial for ponds/borders) rather than from any single explicit 'not a houseplant' statement, since no admissible source addresses houseplant suitability directly.

water_regime keep_moist rests on RHS's imperative cultivation instruction ('Grow in moist to wet deep, humus-rich, acid soil in full sun.') and MoBot's 'constantly moist humusy soils of a border'; no admissible source gives a watering-frequency instruction for this marsh iris, and NC State's 'prefers to grow in rich, moist soils' is a soil descriptor carried as corroboration only.

records.name_note: RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden both lead with 'marsh marigold' on their dedicated pages for this species — RHS pairs the heading 'Caltha palustris' with the common-name subtitle 'marsh marigold', and MoBot's rendered Common Name field carries the single value 'marsh marigold'. NC State does not lead with it: its page title reads 'Caltha palustris (Cowslip, Marsh Marigold, Yellow Marsh Marigold)' and its Common Name(s) field lists those same three entries in that same order, alphabetized, so 'Cowslip' comes first. NC State's own body prose nonetheless names the species 'Marsh marigold' ('Caltha palustris, or Marsh marigold, is a native rhizomatous herbaceous perennial in the buttercup (Ranuculaceae) family...'). 'Cowslip' more usually denotes Primula veris. 'Kingcup' appears on RHS only inside the secondary 'Other common names' field, and on MoBot only inside the Common Name popup, whose text exists solely in the link's markup and is therefore not quoted here.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries a Poison block scoped to humans (its Plant Type list includes "Poisonous" and its Tags include "#poisonous"): Poison Severity is "Low"; Poison Symptoms are "This plant can be toxic and ingesting large amounts of the plant's leaves can lead to burning of the throat, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, dizziness, fainting, and convulsions. No part of this plant should ever be eaten raw."; Poison Toxic Principle is "Protoanemonin"; Causes Contact Dermatitis is "No"; and Poison Part is "Leaves" (the only part listed — not truncated). Separately, NC State's own Edibility field says "Spring greens, in small quantities and properly prepared, for salads," and Missouri Botanical Garden gives edibility/preparation detail with exact conditions: "Flower buds may be cooked and pickled in vinegar for use as a substitute for capers. Young leaves are also edible as cooked greens when boiled. No part of this plant should ever be eaten raw however." No admissible source scopes any toxicity statement to cats or dogs specifically, and the RHS species page for Caltha palustris (rhs.org.uk/plants/2803) carries no toxicity or handling-warning statement at all on this page.
records.cool_rest_note: The plant can go summer-dormant rather than cold-dormant: NC State states "For best flowering, you should site the plant in full sun, however, full sun in the summer may force the plant to go dormant. This can be rectified with a site that provides some afternoon shade in the summer." Missouri Botanical Garden corroborates: "If sited in full sun in hot summer climates such as the St. Louis area, plants may go dormant in summer."
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source scopes any toxicity statement to cats or dogs. NC State's Poison block is explicitly human-scoped ('Poisonous to Humans' heading), and RHS's Caltha palustris species page carries no toxicity statement at all — so there is no cat/dog-scoped evidence to support true or false.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field reads only the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0)', which sets no floor or ceiling per the open-band rule. RHS's Soil pH field is 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', i.e. it lists both alkaline and acid soils as acceptable, which independently rules out setting either a max or a min.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: no admissible source gives day or night temperature ranges for this species; only USDA hardiness zones (NC State: 3a-7b; MoBot: Zone 3 to 7) and an RHS Hardiness rating of H7 are given, and these are zone/survival ratings, not day/night temperature requirements.
chill_damage_f left null: no source states a specific cold-damage-onset temperature; the dormancy behavior documented (NC State, MoBot) is heat-driven summer dormancy, not cold/chill damage.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field only supplies its site-wide legend text ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'), which is boilerplate category definition rather than species-specific footcandle or hour data, so it was not used for these numeric fields.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max left null: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity requirements for this species (it is an outdoor bog/marginal-aquatic plant, not a humidity-sensitive houseplant).
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source provides a fertilizing schedule or dilution guidance for this species.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: this is an in-ground/marginal-aquatic perennial and no source frames its watering in terms of a dry-down target, check depth, or day-interval schedule.

soil_base is recorded as 'garden_bed' by inference from both sources describing in-ground/pond-margin cultivation (RHS: 'Grow in an open site in rich boggy soil at the water's edge'; NC State: landscape uses including 'water gardens, pond edges, rain gardens, and wet, boggy areas') rather than any container or specialty potting-mix description; no enum value for 'bog garden' exists so 'garden_bed' is the closest fit.

The RHS species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/2803/caltha-palustris-marsh-marigold-boots/details) was checked for a toxicity or handling-warning statement and none is present on that page; a harmful-if-eaten or skin-irritant line attributed to RHS in general search-engine summaries did not appear on this specific verified species page and so was not used.

NC State's structured 'is often confused with' module lists Calla palustris and Ranunculus ficaria, while the page's separate body prose instead names Ficaria verna and Geum radiatum as look-alikes/alternatives; both are reproduced here only for transparency and were not used to support any schema field.

Aggressive-spread statements (not a schema field, recorded for reference): NC State: 'This plant will form large colonies over time and can be propagated by seed or root division.' Missouri Botanical Garden: 'Unrestrained rhizomes will spread to form colonies.' Clemson: 'it tends to spread and form large colonies when it's happy, so beware' and 'be aware that it can form large colonies.'
